1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Modern Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6.background: The more “tactical” of the two main branches of the Scandinavian Defence, known as the Modern Scandinavian. John Emms calls 3.d4 White's main line against it.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4.strategy: The main line. White gives up the idea of keeping the pawn and takes central space instead, opening lines for the queen and the c1-bishop. Black wins the pawn back, so the game turns on whether White's bigger centre outweighs Black's quick, comfortable development.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4.name: Scandinavian Defence: Modern Variation

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4.strategy: Defends the d5 pawn with a pawn and tries to keep the extra material instead of handing it back. The cost is that the c4 pawn blocks the f1-bishop's diagonal and gives Black a target: the pawn chain can be chipped away at once, and White often has to return the pawn anyway.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 c6.strategy: The most common reply: the c-pawn attacks d5 from the side and aims to open the centre. If White grabs on c6, Black recaptures with a knight and has a lead in development for the pawn, so White normally returns the pawn with a central strike, which gives an equal game.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 c6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Panov Transfer

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 e6.strategy: A gambit for speed: if White takes on e6, Black's bishop recaptures with development and hits the c4 pawn. Black hopes that an open position and a lead in development outweigh the pawn, but against calm play it is simply a pawn down.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 e6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Icelandic-Palme Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 e6.background: Invented by Icelandic masters who looked for an alternative to the more common 3...c6.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5.strategy: The natural reply: Black wins the pawn back at once with a knight that is already developed, so no time is lost. The knight stands in the centre but can be driven off by c4 while White builds a bigger centre, so Black has to avoid ending up cramped.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4.strategy: Develops with an attack on the queen and does not hurry to recapture. White can keep the extra pawn, so this is a real gambit: Black bets on quick development and active pieces, and the game is sharp from the start.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6.strategy: A less direct way to regain the pawn: the c-pawn attacks d5 a third time and keeps Black's set-up compact, but it spends a move on a pawn instead of developing a piece. Sound, but Black is a step behind in development compared with the main reply.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6.strategy: A rare fianchetto: the bishop on g7 will press on d4 from a distance instead of developing in front of White's central pawns. Black leaves d5 alone for the moment, so White can secure the extra pawn and the space with c4.
